title: The Big Bounce
full_review:
A two-bit thief is recruited by a well-connected judge and a thrill-seeking temptress to double-cross a shady real estate developer in the cringe-worthy caper comedy, "The Big Bounce" (Warner Bros.).

Situated strategically between the year-end rush of Oscar contenders and summer slew of blockbusters, January and February have traditionally been the months during which studios try to unload their duds onto moviegoers willing to fork over cash for just about anything to get out of the cold. After Tinseltown cleaned out its fridge, providing a holiday season feast of epics and nuanced character pieces, director George Armitage serves up what can only be described as cinematic leftovers.

Based on a novel by dime-store crime icon Elmore Leonard, the film stars Owen Wilson as Jack Ryan, a slacker, surfer, charmer and all-around trouble magnet who, after drifting about as far west as one can go without a pocket full of yen, finds himself working construction in Hawaii for Ray Ritchie (Gary Sinise), a slimy resort magnate. After a run-in with Ray's pit-bull foreman (Vinnie Jones) and his flunky (Charlie Sheen) lands him in jail, a local magistrate (Morgan Freeman), intrigued by the petty pilferer, offers Jack a handyman job at the Oceanside condo complex he owns.

The paradisiacal playground offers more than enough temptations for a man of Jack's predispositions, including Nancy Hayes (Sara Foster), a sultry island seductress who just happens to be Ray's mistress. It doesn't take long for Jack to get the itch, and Nancy is just the girl to scratch it. She quickly lures Jack out of his clothes and into a scam which will score them $200,000 of Ray's money, setting the stage for the elaborate shell game of double and triple dealings one has come to expect from Leonard adaptations.

Despite the picturesque Hawaiian backdrop provided by Oahu's North Shore, the silly story is shakier than a hula dancer's hips, full of awkward reversals and plot twists. Unlike the wickedly funny "Get Shorty" (1995), which was also based on a novel by Leonard, "Bounce" lacks, well, bounce, resulting in a flat-line black comedy, more pallid than it is pulp, which not even Leonard's whip-smart dialogue can resuscitate.

During the movie's opening voiceover, Jack blames his albatross karma on his two constant traveling companions: "bad luck" and "bad choices"; the latter companion must be two-timing it with the actor playing him, as evident in Wilson's poor choice of scripts.

However, while Wilson is competent as the likable loser, the same cannot be said for Foster, a former model with the acting range that profession usually implies, who prances through most of her scenes scantily clad in string bikinis or less -- justifying the film's buoyant title.

The remaining cast, made up of such impressive players as Sinise, Freeman, Sheen and Bebe Neuwirth, who plays Ray's conniving wife, seem to be just going through the motions as they tag along for the paycheck and excuse to be in Hawaii. You know you're in trouble when the best performance is by the saxophonist punctuating each scene with a jazzy "Harlem Nocturne" riff.

More disconcerting than the insipid script is the film's wink-wink assertion that crime not only pays, but on occasion pays quite well. Though Armitage keeps the tone lighthearted -- the characters are more rogues than hardened criminals -- by the movie's end, Jack and Nancy not only literally get away with murder, but cut a very sweet profit in the process. Also troubling is the atheistic mantra, "God is just an imaginary friend for adults," which is repeated throughout by various characters for supposed comic effect.

Early on, the judge warns Jack, "Things aren't always what they seem." "The Big Bounce" is exactly what it seems -- a big waste of time.

Due to a few sexual encounters with partial nudity, a casual attitude toward murder and larceny, an implied homosexual situation, recurring violence, some crude humor and language, as well as racial slurs, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
